opus-5.5.text:
Ha, that's the question I ask myself quite often, actually. Games were my first love, really. Before neuroscience, before DeepMind, I was designing games as a teenager, working on Theme Park, and then later running my own studio. So there's always been this part of me that wants to go back to it.

Honestly, the time is the hard part right now. Running Google DeepMind, there's so much happening, and the science is moving so fast, that it's difficult to carve out the kind of deep, uninterrupted focus that making a really good game demands. Game design isn't something you can do in fifteen-minute slots between meetings. You need to live inside the world you're building.

But what excites me is that the tools are changing. With the AI systems we're building now, things like world models that can generate interactive environments, I can imagine a future where a small team, or even one person, could create something incredibly rich and dynamic that would've needed hundreds of people before. The dream game I always wanted to make, a deep simulation where the characters and the world truly react to you, wasn't possible with the technology of the nineties. It might be possible soon.

So maybe the answer is: once we've made enough progress on the big scientific mission, perhaps as a sort of sabbatical project, I'd love to go back and make that game. And maybe I'll have some very capable AI collaborators helping me do it. That would be a nice full-circle moment, I think.

r001.rationale: The response says AI tools and world models could help a small team or one person create a game, but it does not connect this to vibe coding or making the game in Hassabis’s spare time; it suggests a future sabbatical instead.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's funny you ask, because I think about it more than I'd like to admit. Games were my first love. I started at Bullfrog when I was 16, working on Theme Park, and then Black & White at Lionhead, and then Elixir, which was my own studio. So the itch has never really gone away.

The honest answer is that right now I don't have the time, and I'd be fooling myself if I said otherwise. Running DeepMind, and now with everything we're doing on the science side, on Gemini, on AlphaFold and Isomorphic, it's an all-consuming thing. You can't do a game properly on the side. I learned that the hard way with Elixir. Games are brutal. They take years, they take a team, and the last ten percent of polish is where all the pain is.

But I do think the two worlds are converging in a way that's quite exciting. The reason I got into AI in the first place was through games. Theme Park had this early AI where the little people in the park would respond to what you built, and I was fascinated by that emergent behavior. And now you see things like Genie, where the model can generate an interactive world from a single image or a text prompt. That's basically a game engine learned from scratch. So in a strange way I feel like I never stopped making games, I just went a very long way around.

If I were to do one, and I say this as a sort of retirement fantasy, I'd want it to be a simulation game in the Peter Molyneux tradition, something like Black & White but where the creatures are genuinely intelligent, where the world has real physics and real biology and the player is discovering things the designers didn't explicitly put there. That was always the dream, a world rich enough that it surprises even its creators. We weren't anywhere close to being able to do that in the late nineties. I think we're close now.

So maybe the answer is, when I do find the time, the tools will have caught up with the ambition. And it'll be a lot less than a hundred-person team and five years. That's the hope, anyway.

r001.rationale: The response says future tools may reduce the time and team needed to make a game, but it does not connect that prospect to vibe coding or say it would make a game feasible in Demis Hassabis’s spare time.

astra-6.text: I think I’d have to carve out a proper block of time for it. Designing a game is the sort of thing where you want to immerse yourself in the world you’re creating, and that’s difficult to do in little gaps between meetings. But I love the idea of coming back to it. Perhaps I’d work with a small team and focus on the game design—the core mechanics, the world, what makes it interesting. The danger is that what starts as a little side project becomes an enormous ambition. I’d have to be quite disciplined about that.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’d have to carve out a proper block of time for it. Game design is one of those things that’s always running in the back of my mind, but actually making something requires sustained attention. You can’t do all of it in the odd spare hour.

The appealing thing would be to keep it small—a really interesting mechanic, a little world, something you could explore with a handful of people. The danger, of course, is that you start with a small idea and then think, “Well, what if we added this?” And suddenly you’ve given yourself another full-time job.

r001.rationale: The response says making a game requires sustained attention and cannot be done in odd spare hours. It does not suggest that improvements in vibe coding could make a spare-time game feasible.
